name: Quantum-Centric Chemistry Beyond Exact Diagonalization (IBM Heron + Fugaku)
algorithm: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with classical supercomputer post-processing
description: Quantum-centric supercomputing benchmark coupling an IBM Heron quantum processor with the Fugaku classical supercomputer to compute ground-state electronic structure of molecules beyond what exact diagonalization can reach: N2 dissociation and [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] iron–sulfur clusters. Circuits used up to 77 qubits and 10,570 two-qubit gates; the classical side applied sample-based quantum diagonalization to project noisy quantum samples onto chemically meaningful subspaces. This is one of the first end-to-end benchmarks of the quantum-centric-supercomputing architecture on a real chemistry target set.
hardware: IBM Heron superconducting processor + RIKEN Fugaku supercomputer
significance: Extends quantum chemistry benchmarks past the exact-diagonalization frontier onto iron–sulfur clusters — a biologically relevant, historically hard target — inside a credible quantum-classical workflow.

news.title: IBM, RIKEN and NVIDIA report 79-fold SQD accuracy gain on iron-sulfur cluster
news.excerpt: IBM Quantum, RIKEN and NVIDIA ran sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) for the [Fe4S4(SCH3)4]2- iron-sulfur cluster using 88 active qubits on ibm_kingston, paired with RIKEN's GB200-based ROQUO supercomputer. Seeding SQD with broken-symmetry unrestricted Hartree-Fock reference states gave a 79-fold improvement in energy accuracy over earlier RHF-seeded SQD work, with an extrapolated energy 0.33 mHa from the extrapolated DMRG value.

news.title: Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM extend quantum-centric chemistry to 12,000-atom protein-ligand complexes
news.excerpt: A Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM collaboration, a 2026 Gordon Bell Prize finalist, used two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors (up to 94 active qubits) with Fugaku, Miyabi-G and ROQUO to compute fragment energies for trypsin-benzamidine (12,635 atoms) and T4-lysozyme with n-butyl-benzene (11,608 atoms). The team reports a more than 40x increase in molecular size over the earlier 303-atom Trp-cage study and up to a 210x improvement in fragment energy accuracy over prior quantum-embedding benchmarks.
